An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.
A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries.
It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.
The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.
The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.
They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.
On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.
US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.
Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".
Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".
The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attack and the BBC has been unable to verify this claim.
Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners.
Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals. The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport.
There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that.
The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions.
The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control.
Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border.

7b949f612db2.text: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/at-least-139-migrants-dead-dozens-missing-after-boat-capsizes-off-djibouti-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter At least 139 migrants dead, dozens missing after boat capsizes off Djibouti coast World Oct 11, 2026 2:05 PM EDT GENEVA (AP) — At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via the phone. "What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened." Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded." "The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore." A pair of shoes believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore after a boat carrying about 305 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, Photob by Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Handout via Reuters. He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support. "They're all in a state of shock," Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. "I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult." Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise. Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait. "This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities." In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia. Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project. "No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down." Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. 48505cbfb184.text: By — Sheikh Saaliq, Associated Press Sheikh Saaliq, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/leaders-from-indias-cockroach-movement-released-from-detention-pledge-to-hold-more-protests Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Leaders from India's 'Cockroach' movement released from detention, pledge to hold more protests World Oct 11, 2026 3:08 PM EDT NEW DELHI (AP) — Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after being released from detention, a day after police cracked down on demonstrations against a controversial revision of voter lists. The movement is demanding the resignation of the country's election chief. The protests were triggered after authorities removed more than 130 million voters from the list since last year. Critics say the move is politically motivated. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny manipulation allegations. The Cockroach Janata Party's three leaders — Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year," Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests. Police boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi. After his release, Dipke called Modi "an embarrassment to India." "Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X. Security personnel detain protesters during a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, near the protest site in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. Photo by Adnan Abidi/Reuters. Das, a spokesperson for the movement, urged supporters to take to the streets. "A situation has been created where the state is at war with its own citizens," he told reporters Sunday. Following Saturday's protests, authorities launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers. Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city. Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said. Small groups of protesters returned to the Indian capital on Sunday, staging marches across the city. The police quickly broke up most of the demonstrations, detaining some protesters again. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner. Modi's party has said the voter revision is needed to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries. The Cockroach movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years. Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.
Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.
The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.
While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El NiÃ±o ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.
Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.
Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.
Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.
Mama Lifa and her child Lifa were found in a patch of acacia trees entirely surrounded by oil palm plantations.
The degradation of their habitat by wildfires as well as a lack of food sources prompted their rescue in mid-September.
Mama Man and her baby, Man, had been monitored by animal rescuers since June, when they were found living in a plantation area adjacent to a small patch of forest.
Fires that spread near to the site restricted their roaming area further, leaving them without a safe route to other forestry. The threat of exposure to the blazes led to them being evacuated in early September, Yiara said.
The reserve these orangutans were released into was chosen because it there is food and water available and it is connected to other forested areas.
Yiari's Argitoe Ranting said: "We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat."
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that wildfires were burning in habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population.
It says a large portion of the ape's habitat will become inhospitable to them if climate change continues at its current pace.
This year's El NiÃ±o has become the strongest on record and is expected to have a knock-on effect on the climate into next year.
Experts have also pointed to land-clearing practices used to make room for plantations as another factor facilitating the spread of wildfires in Indonesia, with naturally fire-resistant forests replaced by less dense and shaded vegetation.
That the orangutan's original habitats had been burned and fragmented to the point they could no longer sustain the primates was the main driving factor behind relocating them, Yiara said.

e42c77375593.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-to-undergo-surgery-to-remove-nodule-on-his-lung Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove nodule on his lung World Oct 11, 2026 2:34 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery "in the coming days" to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week. The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers. The Vatican didn't say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it. A nodule can be benign or malignant A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. "Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. "When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said. A statue of the late Pope John Paul II outside the entrance to Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is expected to undergo surgery this week to remove a small growth on his lung, in Rome, Italy, October 11, 2026. Photo by Matteo Minnella/Reuters. If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview. "It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread," he said. Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go. In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, "doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it." He thanked the faithful "for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers." Surgery to be at the pope's hospital Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man. Francis' illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope's health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days. This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay. Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted. A nodule doesn't mean cancer but should be investigated Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn't mean lung cancer. And in fact "a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer." But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. "The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule," he said in an interview. Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said. "In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery," he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications. Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking. Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. f2bcbb9da01f.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/bipartisan-group-of-senators-calls-on-trump-to-reverse-course-on-russian-diesel-plan Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Bipartisan group of senators calls on Trump to 'reverse course' on Russian diesel plan Politics Oct 11, 2026 4:18 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., speaks in Concord, New Hampshire, in 2024. Photo by Elizabeth Frantz/ Reuters The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. "We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. "Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law." Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. "The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation." He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. "This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices. Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in their war, with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but no comment from Moscow.
The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially told a US media outlet that it was "news" to him, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He has also accused Russia of striking Ukraine's energy facilities after Trump posted his announcement.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The diesel deal has been criticised by Zelensky, some European officials and some US politicians, including some from Trump's Republican party.
After Trump claimed an energy truce had taken effect, Zelensky expressed surprise to news site Axios before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".
"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.
The BBC has asked the White House for further details.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now".
French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have also expressed their support for an energy truce.
After speaking to von der Leyen, Zelensky said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power outages, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.
In Ukraine, six people have been killed in Russian attacks on two cities, regional officials said.
A person has been killed in Russia's Belgorod region, according to its regional task force.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.
Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.
The deal announced with Russia earlier this week, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
The US-Israeli war with Iran has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's oil products usually flow - and pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.
That conflict has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
Zelensky has called the diesel deal a gift to Putin. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has told the BBC that the UK did not support it. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has echoed Zelensky's comments.
Some US politicians - including some from Trump's Republican party - have also criticised the deal.
Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal with Russia "runs directly counter" to a law that banned Russian energy imports.
"Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," the statement said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.
Following Zelensky's criticism, Trump accused the Ukrainian leader of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries and said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Zelensky responded by pledging to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.
The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.
Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.

5c6f7c534f7b.text: By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/riyadh-airport-hit-by-projectile-a-day-after-deadly-missile-strike Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Riyadh airport hit by projectile a day after deadly missile strike World Oct 11, 2026 3:49 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others. Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday. The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday. India's embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also had been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport, after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 8, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. Social Media/via Reuters. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back. Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts. "There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference. He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details. Houthis have targeted Saudi air, military and oil facilities Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday. The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods. The dead in the airport attack included several nationalities Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant for Saudi airline Flynas identified as Azza Ramzy, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother who had been living in Saudi Arabia, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Iran can use the Houthis to pressure a key US ally Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the Iran war's sidelines, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now, they are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. 80d8c147cbf3.text: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

06daf636c421.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Elise Morton, Associated Press Elise Morton, Associated Press By — Collin Binkley, Associated Press Collin Binkley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-claims-russia-and-ukraine-agree-to-energy-ceasefire-despite-continued-attacks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire' despite continued attacks World Oct 11, 2026 5:25 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement. Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!" Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv. "Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening." The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia." Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter." Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world." He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. "We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ." On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal. Trump spars with Zelenskyy Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. "Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made. "With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added. Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in. The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line. Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure. He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort. Ukrainian strike on Russian data center triggers outages The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra. "Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability. Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.
Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday.
Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented.
Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border.
Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region.
"The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes."
It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise.
The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured.
Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.
The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.
Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.
At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.
Gold lies at the core of the border tensions.
Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders.
Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels.
Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.
Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.
This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.

People are being told to prepare for "the unthinkable" as flood response teams warn of a heightened risk over the autumn.
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it was concerned by long-range forecasts, external which indicated an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual over the coming months.
Those living in flood-hit areas told BBC Wales they were worried, and had started preparing.
One in seven properties in Wales is classed as being at risk of flooding, but NRW said just 27% of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.
After a summer marked by drought and wildfires, the organisation has urged people "not to become complacent" and said conditions could change quickly.
Wales has seen a series of major floods in recent years, often in the wake of powerful storms such as Dennis in 2020, Bert and Darragh in 2024 and Claudia in 2025.
The threat comes from both rivers and the sea, while surface water flooding - where local drainage systems become overwhelmed during heavy downpours - is seen as an increasing danger.
NRW argues that the country's geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and several so-called "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.
More than 274,500 homes and businesses are currently classed at risk of flooding, with this figure set to increase significantly by the end of the century.
'People could have died'
On the high street in Monmouth, people told BBC Wales of "harrowing" and "dreadful" scenes when major flooding hit in November 2025.
Friends Malcolm Butcher, 82, Jim Tyler, 81, Brian Churches, 82 and Dave Blake, 82, said they had lived in the town all their lives "and never seen anything like it".
"At 2:30 in the morning when it hit it was unbelievable... absolutely raging," Malcolm said.
If it had happened in the daytime "people would have died", he added.
Eighteen cars on his road were lost to the flood waters - including his own, while the houses in the street behind were all flooded out.
"It is a worry, we have three rivers running into Monmouth... and the winters are changing," he said.
People could help prepare for floods by moving "the good stuff upstairs" and making sure they had sandbags to hand ahead of bad weather, he said.
"It's not back to normal yet but we're getting there," added Imogen Elliot, 82.
"Waitrose was four feet in water and it went right up the street - we've had flooding before but not like that."
Jane Roche, who runs a cafÃ© and fishmongers on the banks of the River Teifi in Cardigan, Ceredigion, has helped coordinate a community flood plan for the area.
"Flooding is something we've learned to live alongside for many years - we've seen first-hand the disruption it can cause for businesses, residents and visitors," she said.
"Developing a community flood plan has brought local people together, helped us understand what actions we need to taken when warnings are issued and given us confidence to support one another when severe weather is forecast."
More frequent and intense weather extremes are expected as a result of climate change, with Wales facing the prospect of wetter, wilder winters more often.
Meanwhile, this year scientists are monitoring the El NiÃ±o event over the Pacific Ocean - which set to be "strongest in living memory".
The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather.
While this does not automatically translate into bad weather in the UK it is "part of the picture" that is leading to concerns for the coming months, according to Jeremy Parr of NRW.
"We do invest in flood defences... but you can't stop all of the flooding all of the time," he said.
"So that means that people need to think the unthinkable really - or the unpleasant - and [consider] if it were to flood around where I live, what would I do?"
"Time and time again" the organisation was told by people who had experienced devastating flooding that "they'd never flooded before, and didn't think it would happen to them", he added.
NRW advises people to check their flood risk by postcode online, external, sign up for flood warnings and access advice about what to do, external if flooding is forecast in their area.
The organisation's flood warning service is available to 181,158 properties in Wales, but new figures show just 48,844 were currently signed up to receive the alerts via phone or email.
"It is low - 27%," Parr admitted, suggesting that people may be being put off by myths that signing up could affect their insurance premiums.
Cardigan's mayor Olwen Davies has bought a flood door for her own house, and also uses a flood gate for extra protection.
She said: "The river comes up once or twice a year... if there's a high tide, with a strong south-westerly wind that's what creates the most havoc.
"We work together and we know who to call on," she said.
Sarah Davies from the Met Office said long-range forecasts for October, November and December suggested "a greater chance of weather-related disruption".
"Weather patterns can change quickly at this time of year, and long-range forecasts describe broad seasonal trends rather than the timing, location and severity of individual weather events," she added.
"Whatever the season, understanding your flood risk and knowing what action to take if warnings are issued are sensible steps that can help you prepare should severe weather occur."
Additional reporting by Sara Dafydd

30aebde30d7c.text: By — Sophie Bates, Associated Press Sophie Bates, Associated Press By — Kate Brumback, Associated Press Kate Brumback, Associated Press By — Julie Walker, Associated Press Julie Walker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/isaias-moves-north-as-rachel-batters-southern-california Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Isaias moves north as Rachel batters Southern California Nation Oct 11, 2026 4:44 PM EDT PENSACOLA, Fla. (AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Isaias swept through as the storm's remnants brought the risk of flooding to the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region on Sunday. Meanwhile, significant waves from Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California. "Major coastal flooding has already been occurring in some areas, with observed water levels running as much as 1.5 feet above predictions," the National Hurricane Center said, noting that high waves are coinciding with high tides. In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. Tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina, and life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts. At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north. In Florida's Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city's fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state's emergency management agency. Heavy rains cause problems in North Carolina In Burke County, North Carolina, an unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton. People ride a golf cart through a partially flooded parking lot in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Gulf Breeze, Florida, U.S., October 10, 2026. Photo by Marco Bello/Reuters. In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks. "Despite a challenging night, we are thankful to report no known injuries or loss of life. We call that a success!" the county emergency management agency posted online. Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals at 9 a.m. Sunday, from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The National Weather Service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible. Dealing with Isaias aftermath in Florida Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city's mayor said the airport "took some damage." The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach. At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out. A drone view shows a damaged apartments building in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, US, October 11, 2026. Photo by Marco Bello/Reuters. With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it's hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies. "Anything that they're willing to give us is helpful," she said. While her home didn't suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. "The biggest thing is our food going bad. It's really hard to keep grilling everything and then where do we store all this food?" Roughly 356,000 customers were without power Sunday at 2:30 p.m. ET in southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, according to poweroutage.com. Sarah Gatewood, a spokesperson for Florida Power & Light, said workers from all over Florida and from more than two dozen other states were mobilized to help restore power. Rachel brings wind and rain to southern California and the Southwest Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing unusually big waves to Southern California, and it dissipated over Las Vegas as it drenched deserts across the Southwest. Waves battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September. "This area is completely shattered and vulnerable," Jack Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said. "The fact that Rachel came and gave it the knockout blow — I don't want to say it can't get any worse for these houses, but it's really, really sad." 71124c1fd9ef.text: By — Fernando Llano, Associated Press Fernando Llano, Associated Press By — Martin Silva, Associated Press Martin Silva, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/hurricane-simon-hits-mexicos-pacific-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast with damaging winds and rain World Oct 11, 2026 6:01 PM EDT PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. The U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall, which could enable it to maintain its dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 140 mph (220 kph). That's not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm. By midday Sunday, Simon's eye was moving within about 65 miles (100 kilometers) of Cabo Corrientes at about 7 mph (11 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillipe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific. Waves hit the waterfront as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, October 11, 2026. Photo by Daniel Becerril/Reuters. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 25 miles (35 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 80 miles (130 kilometers) from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected. "We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells." Meanwhile, the hurricane dumped rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 centimeters) of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters). As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders. Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads. "Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote. Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated. Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting. "It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again." Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta. Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation. "The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone. Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital. "We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Regan Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-calls-latest-u-s-proposal-to-end-war-insufficient-as-netanyahus-corruption-trial-resumes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran calls latest U.S. proposal to end war 'insufficient' as Netanyahu's corruption trial resumes World Oct 11, 2026 5:43 PM EDT A senior Iranian official says Tehran finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war "insufficient" and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country's longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says latest US response is 'insufficient' The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States "insufficient" as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran's state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran's delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened "cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region" if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard's navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be "identified as hostile," according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran's proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday's attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously" about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. "Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes," Abed said. Israel's military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into 'NAZA' documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary "NAZA," in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells "a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel" and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel's actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon's army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was "directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank" and called it "a flagrant violation of existing understandings." An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March. Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".
Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".
Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.
The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.

- Published
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.
In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.
On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.
Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.
Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.
Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.
The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.
Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.
Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.
The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.
"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upchargeâ¦ is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.
That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
