Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.
The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.
But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.
The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.
For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning.
"It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival.
"It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.
The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.
The show was a ratings hit.
But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.
Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy.
"The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said.
"And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."
When asked whether he thinks attitudes towards entertainment have now changed, Pattinson paused.
"I think on mainstream TV, but then it's just been replaced," he replied, pointing out that similar content has since appeared on social media.
"That's why I was interested in the show, because I could see the beginning of a new wave of 'predator catching' in pretty much the same format that it was in the early 2000s," he said. "And I was just interested as to why that was happening."
"And it got bigger and bigger and bigger, and now it's one of the most massive things on social media."
Hansen himself has been critical of the film, calling it "bizarre" and "detached from reality" in a video posted on X, external.
Addressing his criticisms, director Lance Oppenheim said: "I agree, that was by design.
"I always thought of this movie as more of a fever dream than something that was representational portrait."
Oppenheim added there was something "ancient" about the desire to watch people getting publicly punished.
"It's happened for thousands of years," he added. "I wanted to make something that interrogated that."
Oppenheim, who is also currently co-directing with Nathan Fielder a highly anticipated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, said separately of that project: "I want everyone to see it. It's a really special movie."
From Twilight to the Oscars?
Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.
Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.
He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.
This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.
Heâs also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didnât give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")
Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?
"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds.
"But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief has defended a plan to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan, rejecting claims that it could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr.
"I don't see an elevated risk," Markwayne Mullin said on Sunday. "I think people need to understand that if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime."
Hasan, a former US Army Major, is due to be executed by firing squad in December for shooting dead 13 soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Trump administration has said it plans to livestream his death, prompting shock and concern from both Republicans and Democrats.
President Donald Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.
It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.
Alaskan Republican Senator, Lisa Murkowski, called the decision "gruesome" and said livestreaming an execution was something she would expect "from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America".
"It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks," she wrote on X, external, adding that "how we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself."
Virginia Democrat Mark Warner said that allowing the public to tune into the execution could heighten the national security risk.
"Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk," he wrote, external.
But speaking to CBS news programme Face the Nation on Sunday, the DHS secretary rejected these concerns, and insisted the risks had been considered.
"[Hasan] killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies," Mullin told presenter Margaret Brennan.
Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed troops at a crowded medical building at the Fort Hood military base. A further 32 others were injured in the attack.
In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes" and said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.
His execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first execution by firing squad since World War Two.

Who are the Houthis, and why are they so hard to fight?
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed to respond to the attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
It comes after the Houthis fired missiles in strikes across Riyadh, killing at least 14 and injured more than 300 in two strikes on the city's airport. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.

ec7df0b6f44e.text: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." Get the 16-page FGS report .

Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed.
Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year.
The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire.
In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location".
A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external.
Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway.
The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this.
The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it.
These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations.
Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked.
Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater."
Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment".
Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy.
The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand.
"They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated.

71cba14b7542.text: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeevâs job is getting them to stay there.
The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. Heâs also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations.
His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars canât get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI.

After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs. Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year.
Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. âIsraelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but thatâs not the way they view the exchange,â he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview.
âOwning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,â he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AIâs productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israelâs economic weakness, its small population. âThere will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.â
The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasnât an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way âto signal the world that we are part of itâ and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said.
Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but âinvestors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.â

Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldnât do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, weâll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE.
Iâm mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 â is patriotism part of the pitch?
No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But thatâs not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but thatâs not the way they view the exchange.
Then whatâs the pitch?
You are Israeli. You donât understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once youâre ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York.
Youâve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother?
We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that itâs not significant enough, but itâs a free option.
And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. Thatâs money that is just ready to be invested.

I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. The Scene
Riyadh Season â the Saudi capitalâs biggest suite of events that had been key to its tourism push â opens next week with concerts, UFC, the Epcot-esque Boulevard World, and the worldâs top ranked tennis players set to compete at the Six Kings Slam.
Since 2019, it has been the capitalâs answer to anyone asking whether Riyadh is the place to be. After the Houthi strikes over the weekend, residents are asking themselves the same question.
Traffic on King Fahd Road is lighter and some companies â mostly those based in the King Abdullah Financial District â told staff to work from home on Sunday. Schools in the city have moved to remote learning for the week, with no clear date yet on when students will return to class.
When I ask Saudis â friends, relatives, and sources â how they are doing, most say: Alhamdulillah, thanks to God, the catchall for everything from the greatest blessings to the mantra mourners repeat when family members die. Itâs the same expression they used in March when Iranian missiles first reached the capital, but the tone now is different after more than a dozen people were killed and hundreds wounded in attacks on King Khalid International Airport.
Fear is breaking through. Social media and WhatsApp group chats have been filled with eulogies for Captain Hamoud Alkalthami, the Saudia Airlines pilot killed on Thursday, and for Saturdayâs dead â eight of them foreign residents from countries including Bangladesh, Egypt, and Sudan. People are posting about and queuing to donate to blood banks. The crown prince himself did so last week, part of an annual campaign, and that image was used to spur urgently needed donations. The captainâs death in particular has become a symbol for many Saudis: The war now has a martyr, with a name and face that looks like theirs.
Manalâs view
Saudis broadly trust their government. When they wrap themselves in the flag, or share statements of solidarity after attacks (at least for those who use their real names), itâs genuine and reflects how people speak in private.
But there has been a shift. Some are talking about leaving, which a few months ago would have been seen as a betrayal. Most are still confident and say the kingdom has come through worse. Whatâs pretty universal is the desire for the disruption to be over and to get back to living.
While the conflict with Iran was clear â we have been told to be wary of the Islamic Republic from the time we understood what an enemy was â the confrontation with the Houthis is more complex. Riyadh has tried a mix of strikes and diplomacy for more than a decade, and the UN-brokered truce in 2022 held long enough for people to stop thinking about the issue. Itâs clear now that itâs a forever war, and few people I speak to can describe what winning would look like.
Without public polls, itâs impossible to gauge exactly what the Saudis think. Speaking to more than 25 people this weekend showed a split. One camp wants the Houthis finished for good, whatever that may mean. Others worry about the toll on Yemenis, our poorer neighbors, who make up the kingdomâs largest foreign community and share ties of kinship and history with Saudis.
Over the past six months, those who lived through the 1991 Gulf War used it to explain why they werenât worried. Those six weeks of Iraqi strikes had one Saudi business leader âmore frightened of the uncertainty of the Scud than anything else.â Uncertainty is again, 35 years later, the greatest fear.
Notable
- The strikes sharply raise the risk of Saudi Arabia being drawn into a wider war, after a decade in which Riyadh worked to contain the Yemen conflict rather than escalate it, Bloomberg reported.
- Eulogies for the 12 killed in Saturdayâs strike filled Saudi social media, among them a Flynas flight attendant killed on duty and a university student in her final year, Arab News reported.

Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (Â£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.
Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.
It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (Â£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (Â£211m) to make and market.
But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".
The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.
Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of IP-driven hits starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of the Top Gun and Mission: Impossible franchises.
Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (Â£38m) worldwide.
The film would need around $350m (Â£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.
However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (Â£227m).
Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.
The film is directed by Alejandro G IÃ±Ã¡rritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.
Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself".
Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend.
The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (Â£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (Â£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation.
Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (Â£6.8m).
The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices.
The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast.

b5a2377664c2.text: Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies , the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday. Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth. Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time. "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday. What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win. " It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said. The intrigue : Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region. He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity. His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy. Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy. Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income. Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners. Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets. Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth. In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity. Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

An invasive plant said to smell like "rotting meat" has been cleared from a Buckinghamshire river.
More than 2.5km (1.6 miles) of the River Alderbourne has been treated for American skunk cabbage, which is native to swamps and other wetlands in the Pacific Northwest.
BBC Gardeners' World Magazine has described the plant, external as having a smell that resembles "rotting meat".
Environmental charity Groundwork South received Â£9,900 from Affinity Water's INNS Out Scheme to carry out the work.
The team surveyed and treated several locations, including a site at Harding's Row Nature Reserve near Iver Heath.
Surveys conducted after the work showed "promising early results", according to the charity.

d4e5ffdba9d6.text: By — Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press By — Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/watch-2-american-economists-win-nobel-for-studying-how-to-deal-with-economic-shocks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: 2 American economists win Nobel for studying how to deal with economic shocks Economy Oct 12, 2026 9:26 AM EDT STOCKHOLM (AP) — American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. Watch the announcement in the video player above. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. "The laureates' research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before," the Nobel committee wrote. "It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: "It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise." Duo overturned earlier economic assumptions For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. "This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn't,'' said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the "stagflation" of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. "Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,'' the Nobel committee wrote. "Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird's eye view," Hall and Woodford's research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.'' Hall studied consumer choices Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. "If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,'' the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can't borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future "while the rest lived hand to mouth,'' the committee wrote. "The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead," Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. Woodford analyzed how businesses make decisions Woodford's research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. "If the business believes that its competitors' prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation," the Nobel committee wrote. "Businesses' decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.'' Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide "clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.'' Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed "the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending." Economics prize is last Nobel announcement this year The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896. Monday's award was the second Nobel win for a Stanford University professor this year. Dr. Karl Deisseroth shared the medicine prize with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work that led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. Towering coast redwoods are known for their resiliency, withstanding fire, fungus and rot to survive for centuries. But these ancient trees now may be vulnerable to a relatively recent foe: heat waves.
As temperatures climb, photosynthesis slows in these iconic trees, researchers report September 22 in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences. Lab experiments show the rate of the sunlight-driven food making process in its needles roughly halves when temperatures rise from 30° to 40° Celsius.
Such a change usually indicates “severe levels of stress,” says Lily Klinek, an ecophysiologist at the University of California, Davis. That vulnerability can cause tree deaths that may jeopardize one of California’s largest stores of carbon, a shield against climate change.
Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) live only in a narrow strip of coastal habitat from central California to southern Oregon, where temperatures are mild and fog is abundant. But recent heat waves have spiked temperatures in parts of their range to over 40° C.
The impact of heat waves on photosynthesis has been studied in other tree species, with some faring better than others. But this is the first study to investigate how coast redwoods respond to the heat, says Troy Magney, an ecophysiologist at the University of Montana in Missoula.
From July 2022 to October 2024, Klinek, Magney and colleagues repeatedly measured the performance of needles from redwoods in California’s Mendocino County. That period included two heat waves.
Typically, trees stay cool when small porelike openings called stomata allow water to evaporate, taking heat with it, similar to how sweat cools humans. But when conditions get too hot and dry, stomata close, retaining a plant’s moisture. Under extreme heat, the team found that needles reached up to 10 degrees C hotter than the surrounding air due to the dark needles absorbing ample sunlight. That suggests that the stomata were at least partially closed.
Those same pores are crucial for photosynthesis; it’s where the trees take in carbon dioxide — used to make food — and release oxygen. “They could essentially starve if they don’t have access to enough carbon,” Klinek says.
It’s hard to investigate the impact of heat on photosynthesis in the field, though. That would take building a “heat chamber around a real-life branch or wait[ing] for a heat event to happen,” Klinek says. Instead, she climbed onto the roof of her car with a pole pruner and collected samples from about five meters high, in the lower canopy.
In the lab, the researchers subjected the samples to increasing heat to match the heat waves seen in recent summers and measured the resulting photosynthesis rates. Even though the samples were submerged in water, so had their stomata open and had full access to the ingredients for photosynthesis, the rate still declined. “They weren’t slowing their photosynthesis because of carbon starvation,” Klinek says.
For practical reasons, the study focused on younger coast redwoods, not the old growth giants. It’s difficult to reach even the lowest branches on trees more than 100 meters tall. “There are just fundamental limitations on what you can sample if you don’t have a jetpack,” says Christopher Still, an ecophysiologist at Oregon State University in Corvallis who was not associated with the study. Even so, the team’s results show that coast redwoods are “really temperature sensitive. You don’t see this as much with other species necessarily,” Still says.
In the field, Klinek observed trees closing their stomata to preserve water. This suggests that in more realistic conditions, where a heat wave and drought hit simultaneously, lack of heat and water could make the slowdown “even more intense.” But more work needs to be done, she notes. “We still don’t know what the threshold is for irreversible damage.”

A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States.
The US Department of Justice said Ãlvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody.
Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (Â£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest.
He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office.
Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court.
The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (Â£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes".
US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine.
They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US.
They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida.
Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, NicolÃ¡s Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024.
However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed.
Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US.
Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.
The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said but no further details were given.
Omar was born in Somalia and came to the US aged eight fleeing war. First elected to Congress in 2018, she is running for reelection next month, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home. The BBC has contacted Omar for comment.
While the nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time her immigration records have been scrutinised by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", alleging that Omar had previously married her brother "to try to bring him to the United States." Her brother now lives in London, he said.
Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar, a Democrat, denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email.
She has been the target of Trump's insults and the president previously suggested that she "should go back" to Somalia and at times said she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."
Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.
She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote. The timing of Monday's raid â 22 days to the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power for the next two years â is likely to raise concerns from Democrats.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" that it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.

6fac86c786fc.text: By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/what-to-know-about-pope-leos-planned-lung-nodule-surgery Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about Pope Leo's planned lung nodule surgery Nation Oct 12, 2026 10:59 AM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to have an operation this week to remove "a localized nodule" in his lung that was "detected at a very early stage." It is the first medical event of his 17-month papacy. The Vatican said he will be admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday, and predicted a weeklong recovery. READ MORE: Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove nodule on his lung Here's what we know. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. A nodule can be benign or malignant A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (about 1.2 inches) across. It is sometimes detected on a CT scan performed to investigate another problem, such as trauma or a lung infection, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts say the nodule could be benign or malignant and that prompt evaluation is important. If the nodule is cancerous and removed at an early stage, the prognosis is "excellent," and surgery alone may be sufficient treatment, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Leo, 71, is considered otherwise healthy and physically fit, both positive factors for his recovery. He said the nodule was discovered during "recent medical tests," and the Vatican said Monday that no particular health issue prompted the check-up, describing it as "routine." Surgery followed by a week of recovery The Vatican said Leo will be admitted to the hospital on Tuesday in the late morning and undergo surgery in the first days of this week. Oncologists who aren't treating him said patients can often be discharged after just a few days, to recover further at home. The exact date of surgery wasn't released, but Leo had a full slate of audiences and appointments Monday morning and afternoon. WATCH: 'American Pope' traces Leo's journey from Chicago to the Vatican The pope will be treated at Rome's Gemelli hospital, formally known as the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, a nonprofit Catholic teaching hospital that is part of the Catholic Sacred Heart University. The facility has a special apartment set up for pontiffs on the 10th floor that includes a private chapel. Leo's immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was treated there before his May 2025 death during a long illness prompted by a respiratory crisis. St. John Paul II spent so much time at Gemelli that he called it "Vatican III," after the Vatican itself and the papal summer residence at Castel Gandolfo. Upcoming activities and trip in question Leo has several activities scheduled this week. In addition to his regular meetings, he was due to celebrate a public Mass on Wednesday to close a weeklong conference on family ministry. It wasn't known if someone else would celebrate the Mass. Leo also has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is unclear whether the surgery and recovery will affect the ambitious itinerary, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and significant altitude changes in Peru. Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to make the trip. Pope remains in charge, even when unconscious The Vatican has no specific rules governing who takes over if a pope becomes totally incapacitated. Even while unconscious during surgery, Leo remains pope and retains his authority. Pope Francis remained in charge throughout his lengthy hospitalizations, as did St. John Paul II before him. Both made appointments and issued laws and statements from the hospital. A team of officials already handles day-to-day Vatican operations. Medical advances and popes' longer lifespans, however, have highlighted this gap in church law and prompted calls for the Vatican to prepare for a pope becoming too ill or incapacitated to govern. Two days before revealing his planned surgery, Leo confirmed one significant appointment. On Friday, he approved Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as the new dean of the College of Cardinals. Tagle, 69, replaces Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, 92, whose term Francis extended in the weeks before his death. The dean plays a significant role in a papal transition. He presides over the previous pope's funeral and helps lead the cardinals' closed-door meetings before the conclave to discuss the church's future needs. If he is under 80 when the conclave begins, he also presides over the secret election of a new pope in the Sistine Chapel. The Vatican released a letter Leo wrote to Re on Sunday — the day of his announcement — thanking him for his lifelong service to the church. He noted in particular the role that Re played in the recent papal transition, when he celebrated Francis' funeral. "I do not think I am mistaken in saying that you, Your Eminence, have been and remain one of the Holy See's best-known and most esteemed servants," Leo wrote. Barry reported from Milan. Warning: this story contains upsetting descriptions of executions
America's use of the death penalty is under the spotlight once again after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the military would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan.
The former military psychiatrist fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.
His execution would be the first time the US Army had used a firing squad since 1945, a method that several states already authorise to put people to death.
And it comes on the heels of the botched death by lethal injection of Christa Pike - a woman convicted of murdering her classmate.
Pike was taken to hospital and then discharged to prison 10 days later, after making a recovery from the failed attempt, her lawyers said.
Amid rising concerns over botched executions - and renewed federal support for the death penalty - the US has introduced both new and old forms of execution like firing squads, the electric chair and the gas chamber.
Botched executions
The vast majority of executions in the US have been lethal injections since they were first introduced in Texas in 1982. The Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit think tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, says that there have been 64 botched executions, external over the past 50 years - including 51 botched lethal injections - out of a total of 1,683 executions.
The difficulty of carrying out these executions, and the uproar over what some perceive as inhumane treatment, has led officials to consider alternative methods of putting people to death. But medical experts and those who study executions say every method the US uses to put people to death can result in severe pain, especially when botched.
"We always have the possibility that there's going to be a mistake made when human beings are involved in executions," said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.
Several medical groups - including the national associations for doctors and nurses - also ban their members from participating in executions. The American Medical Association, which represents doctors in the US, states they are "a profession dedicated to preserving life when there is hope of doing so" and that participating in any way in executions is antithetical to their oath.
A 'myth' of peaceful lethal injections
Lethal injection, which was first used in Texas in 1982, is now the most common way people are executed across the US, with many states making it their default method.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, said states turned to lethal injection because it appeared from the outside to be a more peaceful means of execution.
"That was a myth," he said.
Dr Zivot said that sometimes the injection of the drugs can cause pulmonary edema, when a person's lungs fill with fluid, which can give people the painful sensation of drowning.
"It's a terrifying way to die - to drown," he said.
Other times, people have medical conditions, like Pike - who suffered from thrombocytosis and other medical problems her lawyers warned about - that can complicate the execution and make it more painful.
During Pike's failed execution, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.
There are a host of reasons why so many lethal injections have been botched, but some of the same factors persist, said Maher.
"Oftentimes, the executions go wrong because training of staff is inadequate, because drugs are degraded or expired or improperly stored, or because states are experimenting with different combinations of drugs that have never been used before," she said.
Most of the time, little information is available to the public about the people administering the lethal injection, as the states do not usually share what training they have had.
"We have discovered that in many instances, and unfortunately subsequent to a botched execution, that the cause was the inadequate experience and training of the execution staff," Maher said.
Drugs for lethal injections are also hard to obtain because many pharmaceutical companies do not want to sell the medications to prisons for that use, since they were developed for life-saving purposes.
New methods like nitrogen gas
In light of many of these challenges, some states have turned to executing people with a new and controversial method: nitrogen gas.
Alabama and Louisiana are the first states to have carried out executions with nitrogen gas, though three other states - Arkansas, Mississippi and Oklahoma - also allow for it.
Two years ago, Alabama used nitrogen gas to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith, after a botched attempt to put him to death via lethal injection in 2022.
During the execution, which took 25 minutes, Smith thrashed violently on the gurney as he was given the gas, a witness told the BBC at the time.
The method involves forcing a prisoner to breathe pure nitrogen gas until they suffocate.
Dr Zivot said people who breathe in the gas sometimes get seizures. Alabama has executed seven people using nitrogen gas since introducing the method in January 2024.
"Each time it was a horror show of struggling, of moving, of seizing," Dr Zivot said.
A return to the electric chair
While some states have explored new methods, others have reauthorised some of the earliest ways US officials used to put people to death.
As of this year, nine states have approved execution by electric chair, with South Carolina using it as their default method.
Electrocution "has a horrible history of botched executions", Maher said, and errors with these executions is one of the reasons why states introduced lethal injections in the first place.
In 1997, Pedro Medina's head caught fire as he was put to death in an electric chair in Florida.

497db1a5418e.text: By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/saudis-probe-how-defense-systems-failed-to-stop-deadly-houthi-attack-on-riyadh-airport Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Saudis probe how defense systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport World Oct 12, 2026 10:47 AM EDT CAIRO (AP) — Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) to reach Riyadh. The incident, one of a string of Houthi attacks since last week on Saudi airports, has exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi Arabia's defense system and signaled a dangerous inflection point in an expanding Mideast conflict that began more than seven months ago when the U.S. and Israel began their war against Iran. READ MORE: Saudi Arabia says 3 injured in attacks on its airports as fighting with Houthis reignites "The events of recent weeks are serious," Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the World Petroleum Energy Congress in Riyadh on Monday. "Our response must be equally serious." The Saudi government-run Center for International Communication, which oversees foreign media, did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the probe into defense failures. Saudi officials want US to engage more actively in countering Houthi attacks On Monday, Saudi state-run media reported that its military was responding to a new attack involving drones and cruise missiles, without providing details. The Saudis are looking to the U.S. to become more directly involved in their fight against the Houthis. The U.S. has provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for a Saudi-led offensive, but so far has held off on directly carrying out strikes against the Houthis. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to try to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The flow of Mideast oil has already been complicated by Iranian efforts to choke off the Strait of Hormuz, another waterway through which about one-fifth of the world's oil flowed before the U.S.-Iran war started in late February. The rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back. President Donald Trump on Saturday told reporters after the deadly airport strike that he was looking at the possibility of carrying out U.S. attacks against the Houthis. READ MORE: Saudi-backed coalition forces Houthis from several areas around key strait, Yemeni officials say But the conflict also comes at a delicate time for Trump, just weeks before U.S. midterm elections that will show whether his Republican Party keeps control of Congress. Persistent inflation and high gas prices fueled by the ongoing conflict with Iran have driven widespread American disapproval of that war. Expanding U.S. military involvement to the Saudi-Houthi conflict comes with the risk of further stoking resentment in the American electorate. Houthis say Saudis launch new attacks Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said Monday that airstrikes on a government complex and a house in the northern province of al-Jawf killed nine people, including five children and a woman, and wounded seven others, according to the Houthi-controlled SABA news agency. Houthi officials also said that Saudi Arabia carried out new strikes on the Yemen capital of Sanaa, killing one person and wounding 12. The Riyadh airport remained closed on Monday and workers in the capital's financial district were told to work from home. Yet, the Saudis on Monday continued with the second day of the World Petroleum Congress. UAE diplomat suggests Gulf allies respond to Houthis jointly Separately, an Emirati diplomat on Monday called for "joint Gulf action" to defend Gulf countries against attacks by Iran and its allied groups. Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the rulers of the United Arab Emirates, said Iran and its allies wrongly assessed that Gulf Arabs were "the weakest link" in the U.S. war against Iran, during which Tehran and its allies repeatedly attacked Arab countries on the other side of the Gulf. "It has become clear that we are all targeted, and that our security is indivisible," he wrote on social media, adding that attacks on Saudi Arabia "undermine the security of the UAE and all Gulf states." Iran's Foreign Ministry on Monday expressed concern about fighting between the Saudis and Houthis and said Iran would be ready to settle disputes between them through diplomacy. Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers reportedly gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.
The chief executive of CoopÃ©rative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.
IntermarchÃ© said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
Some supermarket staff reportedly said they were hit by waves of hot air when they opened freezer units on Monday morning.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of â¬270,000 (Â£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.
The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it had opened an investigation into the incident, which it called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".
Eoropean Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
The full scale of the attack is so far unclear.
Reports in specialist retail and local media said stores from other food giants, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, were also attacked. BBC News has approached the supermarket chains for comment.
In a post on X, CoopÃ©rative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

fcef6a84d355.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ap-report-trump-rubio-weigh-firing-kimberly-guilfoyle-after-mounting-reports-of-improper-conduct Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP report: Trump, Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports of improper conduct World Oct 12, 2026 12:24 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday's Columbus Day holiday. WATCH: 'It was a definite quid pro quo.' GOP donor who accused Guilfoyle of corruption speaks out The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, but in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid. EXCLUSIVE: House Democrats ask Kimberly Guilfoyle for records related to alleged pay-to-play scheme The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations," they said. "Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction. We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action," the lawyers said. After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied. A second U.S. official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied. The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece. Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".
There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".
When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.
Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.
In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.
Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
