85de239bbc7a.text: By — Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/zelenskyy-says-russia-strikes-energy-facilities-despite-trump-claim-of-an-energy-ceasefire Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Zelenskyy says Russia strikes energy facilities despite Trump claim of an energy ceasefire World Oct 12, 2026 12:07 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine's energy facilities even after President Donald Trump said a day earlier that the warring countries had agreed on an energy ceasefire in the 4 1/2-year-old war. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy ceasefire deal with Russia which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same. READ MORE: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire' despite continued attacks "We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side," Zelenskyy said. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's brief social media post on Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!" On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov wouldn't say whether Russia had agreed to such a ceasefire, saying only: "Contacts are ongoing." Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been "horribly surprised" when, following Trump's announcement, Russia struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station. READ MORE: Bipartisan group of senators calls on Trump to 'reverse course' on Russian diesel plan "It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform. Energy strikes have caused pain for both Ukraine and Russia Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either. Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches. Ukraine, meanwhile, has launched strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory. That's prompted Trump to blame Zelenskyy for record U.S. diesel prices — rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran — and to strike a deal with Putin on Friday to import diesel from Russia in an attempt to bring fuel prices down ahead of U.S. midterm elections. READ MORE: Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russian diesel in sharp reversal of U.S. policy ahead of midterms On Monday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, "we will respond." "We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. "This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war." EU foreign policy chief skeptical of energy ceasefire The European Union's top diplomat on Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it. "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg. "Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy." Trump's deal with Putin to purchase diesel from Russia dismayed officials in the U.S., Ukraine and around Europe. A bipartisan group of six senators, including four Republicans, called on the Trump administration on Sunday to "immediately reverse course" on the deal, saying the U.S. should "not provide Putin with a financial lifeline" while Russia is killing Ukrainian civilians. Kallas also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a ceasefire. On Monday, Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night. He added, however, that he would be ready to work towards doing so if Ukraine secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days. In response, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said in a statement that in case of a Ukrainian election, Putin would be ready to halt strikes on Ukraine "specifically on election day," and that Kyiv only wanted a 60-day ceasefire "to gather their strength, heal their wounds, and continue the war." The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.
Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.
APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.
One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.
That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”
Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.
APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.
The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.
The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.
The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.
And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

f0068414c5d8.text: By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/elon-musk-quietly-becomes-biggest-known-donor-in-midterm-contests-as-he-tries-to-save-republicans Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Elon Musk quietly becomes biggest known donor in midterm contests as he tries to save Republicans Politics Oct 12, 2026 11:56 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Elon Musk, the world's only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year's midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress. The numbers, first reported by the New York Times ahead of this week's federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk's super PAC. WATCH: New documentary traces Elon Musk's rise and embrace of right-wing politics The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump in 2024. Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. WATCH: Trump awards Elon Musk the National Medal of Science, among other awards for tech execs It's a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. "I think I've done enough," he said at the time. Republican have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts — a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president's performance, stubbornly high prices and the unpopular war with Iran. Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire mean for Ukraine?
US President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that an energy ceasefire had been reached between Ukraine and Russia that was "effective immediately".
Ukraine's President Zelensky responded by saying his country is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war".
However, Moscow hasn't confirmed its agreement and Zelensky said Russia hit a Ukrainian power plant in Kharkiv "immediately after" Trump's post on Sunday.
The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians are facing another winter with electricity outages that leave people without heat, light or even water.

f2ac98522d6c.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press By — Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/many-gop-states-have-imposed-voting-rules-mirroring-trumps-midterm-proposals Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Many GOP states have imposed voting rules mirroring Trump's midterm proposals Politics Oct 12, 2026 1:27 PM EDT President Donald Trump has pushed Congress to pass a proof-of-citizenship law, signed an executive order seeking a national voter ID requirement and tried to limit mail voting through U.S. Postal Service changes. None of those moves succeeded in time to affect this year's midterm elections. It's a different matter in the states. More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of Trump's stalled proposals. They include changes to what IDs are acceptable to register for the first time and requirements to show proof of citizenship, an issue the Republican president has tried but failed to get through Congress. "Trump's attacks on our elections are deeply damaging, but they are not happening in isolation," said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Voting Rights Project. "Across the country, states are also advancing restrictions that make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot." Republican lawmakers who support the tighter voting laws, especially around voter ID, describe them as common sense changes that help build trust in elections. Trump and other Republicans have been pushing for more restrictive rules since the president's false claims of widespread fraud in his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Trump's false claims have resonated with Republican voters, a majority of whom believe Biden was not legitimately elected despite all evidence to the contrary. Trump lost dozens of court challenges, his own attorney general found no evidence of widespread fraud, and reviews, audits and recounts in the battleground states where he contested his loss all affirmed Biden's victory. Among the changes confronting voters as early voting gets underway: Students in New Hampshire can no longer use student IDs; Utah voters returning mail ballots must include more information on the envelope; and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports to verify their identities. Changes to voter ID requirements are challenged New Hampshire state Rep. Donald McFarlane said he sponsored the bill to eliminate student IDs as acceptable for voting because colleges don't have the same controls when issuing those cards as government agencies. "The change removes a special exception and applies the same government-issued ID standard to all voters," he said, adding that his bill had bipartisan support. Students, he said, can still get state IDs free of charge. The new requirements have not gone unchallenged. In South Dakota, the ACLU has filed a lawsuit seeking to halt a new law that includes requiring voters registering for the first time to present the most common forms of ID — driver's licenses, Tribal IDs and non-driver state IDs. They must be presented in person at places that accept registration. "Proof of citizenship in itself is not terrible," said Kathryn Johnson, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota. Her concern is the requirement to present the IDs in person. "We're kind of a remote state, so sometimes it takes a drive, and you have to coordinate, you have to take off work, and all of these kinds of things," she said. Some Democrats also have expressed support for voter ID during recent debates. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he was open to the idea as long as it wasn't based on "conspiracy theories." When legislatures change their state's voting laws, they typically give election offices and voters time to adjust. Trump wanted federal voter ID and proof-of-citizenship legislation to take effect immediately, forcing election officials and voters to comply in the middle of the midterms. Ohio seeks to scrub voter rolls Ohio has a proof of citizenship requirement in effect for the first time this year for those registering to vote or updating their voter registration information at a Bureau of Motor Vehicles location. The state also eliminated its four-day grace period for mail ballots, which now must be received at local election offices by Election Day. Yet the biggest concern for voting rights groups is an ongoing purge of the state's voter rolls. The databases used to check citizenship against voter registration lists can be outdated, said Freda Levenson, legal director of the ACLU of Ohio, which has sued to overturn the law. "Vast numbers of perfectly eligible voters are vulnerable to being disenfranchised," she said. Republican state Sen. Theresa Gavarone, one of the primary sponsors of the bill, challenged the ACLU's legal action and said the problem it addresses is a real one. "In the past two years, hundreds of noncitizens have been removed from Ohio's voter rolls," she said in an email. "Every single vote cast by a noncitizen disenfranchises a lawful Ohio voter." Voters have mixed views on the changes Outside an early voting center in Wayne County, Ohio, retired steel worker Dan Walter, an independent voter, said he opposes requiring documentary proof of citizenship to vote. "It's to keep people from voting, it sounds to me like," he said. His wife, Jody, a retired aerospace executive and a Democrat, said she felt the same way about Ohio's new requirement for registering to vote. "A driver's license doesn't prove citizenship, and that's all they ask for now," she said. "It's going to be an obstacle for so many people." WATCH: What the Supreme Court's voter-citizenship database decision means for the midterms Genia Fortune had a different view. A nurse, t

035b158bdd68.text: Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise. Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising. The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own. Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication. Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities. Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet. Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself. The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier. What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it." Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases. Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday. Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran." Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso , backed the deal. How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban. GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers , have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war. Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity. His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots. Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion . A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved. Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers. The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

0a4475eaea05.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the UK House of Commons Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was "almost certainly" behind the suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford base where U.S. bombers were stationed. Why it matters: This was the first time the UK officially blamed Iran for the alleged planned attack. What he said: "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. Driving the news: Ten days ago, the U.S. evacuated a dozen B-1 strategic bombers from RAF Fairford in response to intelligence indicating an Iranian drone attack. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen move by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential to dramatically escalate the war in the Middle East. The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. It was unclear whether the people who were arrested were connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel provided the UK with intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. State of play: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the Iranian ambassador was summoned to the foreign office in London to denounce the alleged Iranian plot. What they're saying: The U.S., UK and 27 other western countries published a joint statement on Monday condemning Iran for "use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners." The group said the threat against RAF Fairford "demonstrates the IRGC's continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors."

Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed scrutiny to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid. Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "intimidation" campaign. READ MORE: AP report: Federal agents search Rep. The nature and scope of the investigation were unclear, though officials in President Donald Trump's administration have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have repeatedly drawn criticism from Republicans and senior Trump officials. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that there was an "ongoing investigation" related in part to whether Omar lied on her immigration forms and that "something's going to happen." Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search of her home took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot for reelection. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family. Trump has frequently targeted Omar Trump and fellow Republicans from the highest ranks of party leadership have repeatedly and publicly criticized the Somali-born Omar over her status as an immigrant to the U.S. and her left-wing views. Trump as recently as this past weekend brought up Omar at a rally in Tennessee, where he attacked her upbringing and suggested that Vice President JD Vance "and our people" were investigating her. Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud — an allegation she has denied — and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate her. The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area but provided no other details. The street was blocked off Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home. "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the department said. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department. Omar has long been a target for Republicans Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota's 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced recently to 14 months in prison. Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies." "It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May. "So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime." US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".

afa9df0da734.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/kremlin-relishes-in-u-s-russia-diesel-deal-and-trumps-criticism-of-zelenskyy Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kremlin relishes in U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy World Oct 12, 2026 2:12 PM EDT A deal between Moscow and Washington over exports of Russian diesel and fresh U.S. criticism of Ukraine's leader mark important political victories for the Kremlin, reversing years of sanctions for its full-scale invasion of its neighbor. While the size of Russia's diesel exports is relatively small and unlikely to significantly impact prices, the revenue will help Moscow replenish its war coffers and — more importantly — undermine efforts by Kyiv and its European allies to put up a united front against President Vladimir Putin. Along with President Donald Trump suggesting that Ukraine should get a new leader to replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the developments strengthen the Kremlin's hand at a critical junction of the war, amid relentless attacks by Russia on energy systems and other vital infrastructure. Ahead of next month's midterm elections, Trump blamed a spike in diesel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, even though the U.S.-led war in Iran has sent global energy prices soaring. Mark Galeotti, a Russia expert who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, described the deal that Trump announced Friday as an "astonishing birthday present" for Putin, two days after he turned 74. While Russia's diesel exports could be a "drop in the ocean compared with actual overall demand," Galeotti said it was "a gift for Putin, even if a single barrel of diesel is not exported." That's because "it drives another and increasingly thick wedge between Trump and Zelensky," he said in a podcast on Sunday. Russian strikes continue despite Trump's 'energy truce' Even though Trump declared Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an "energy truce" effective immediately, Russia continued attacking Ukraine's energy facilities, said Zelenskyy, who has criticized the diesel deal as a show of weakness. Zelenskyy emphasized that he is open to an energy ceasefire if it includes a halt to Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid. Russia has not said whether it agrees to such a ceasefire, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday only that "contacts are ongoing." Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov shrugged off Zelenskyy's comments as an attempt "to promote his interest in a ceasefire." READ MORE: Bipartisan group of senators calls on Trump to 'reverse course' on Russian diesel plan "I don't think he deserves a respite," Lavrov said. Galeotti predicted that Putin is unlikely to halt attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities, which he sees as "absolutely central to his winter air war strategy." Russia stepped up aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent months with ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Kyiv's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors whose stockpiles have been drained by the war in Iran. Putin has repeatedly emphasized that Moscow wants a comprehensive, long-term agreement, not a temporary halt to hostilities. Asked to comment on Zelenskyy's statement that Ukraine needs a minimum of 60 days to prepare elections, Peskov said Putin could order a ceasefire only on the day of voting. Russia's fuel crisis causes doubts about export capacity In recent months, Ukraine launched successful aerial attacks that knocked out over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. The strikes caused a severe fuel crisis with long lines at gas stations, bringing the war home to millions. Ukraine also methodically struck oil terminals at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk and targeted dozens of tankers at sea, seeking to derail Moscow's oil exports and drain Moscow's revenues. Putin acknowledged the damage but noted that Moscow is capable of inflicting much bigger blows to Ukraine. Some officials and analysts questioned whether Russia will be able to provide diesel supplies under the deal announced by Trump. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski voiced doubts about it, saying that even the Russian capital is experiencing fuel shortages. Others say Moscow actually has a surplus of diesel, now that demand has eased following the end of the harvest season. "Russia planned to export more diesel anyway," said Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia Division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. Still, some Russian motorists exhausted by months of waiting at gas stations were worried the new deal could leave fewer supplies for the domestic market. "I don't think that's very good, because you can see what's going on at gas stations — people are standing in line around the clock," said Marat Salavatov, waiting to refuel at a Moscow gas station. Russian officials sought to quell such fears, saying there will be enough supply to keep the domestic market stable. The volume of production is able "to fully satisfy the needs of the local market while delivering the agreed amounts to the global market," Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in a government statement announcing the lifting of the diesel export ban that had been in place since July. Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy is seen as aiding Russia In addition to the diesel deal, Trump unleashed biting criticism of Zelenskyy that marks perhaps the lowest point in their relationship since the disastrous Oval Office meeting in February 2025. That could be even more important for the Kremlin. Trump's remark that it was time for a new president in Ukraine and his suggestion that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war topped the news on Russian state television and was widely discussed by pro-Kremlin commentators and military bloggers. cc687c542caf.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/what-is-indigenous-peoples-day-3-things-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What is Indigenous Peoples Day? 3 things to know Nation Oct 12, 2026 1:46 PM EDT Indigenous people celebrate their centuries-long history of resilience with ceremonies, dances and speeches. Former President Joe Biden officially commemorated Indigenous Peoples Day in 2021. An increasing number of states and cities have also recognized it — pivoting from a day long rooted in the celebration of explorer Christopher Columbus to one focused on the people whose lives and culture were forever changed by colonialism. Here is a look at why it's called Indigenous Peoples Day and how people celebrate. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Why is it called Indigenous Peoples Day? Indigenous Peoples Day has been recognized for decades in different forms and under a variety of names to celebrate their history and culture and to recognize the challenges they continue to face. Biden had said in a statement that the day is meant to "honor America's first inhabitants and the Tribal Nations that continue to thrive today." It is typically observed on the second Monday in October, the same day as Columbus Day, a federal holiday established decades ago to recognize Columbus' sighting in 1492 of what came to be known as the Americas. The day is often marked by protests against memorials to Christopher Columbus, for environmental justice, for the return of Indigenous lands and in honor of missing and murdered Indigenous women. President Donald Trump has said he will not follow his predecessor's practice of recognizing Indigenous Peoples Day alongside Columbus Day in October. Is Indigenous Peoples Day a federal holiday? Although it is not a federal holiday, some states, as well as Washington, D.C., have holidays honoring Indigenous people, some of which are on the second Monday in October. Indigenous Peoples Day is typically paired with Columbus Day or replaces the federal holiday altogether. A number of cities and school systems observe Indigenous Peoples Day as well. Indigenous people have campaigned for years for recognition "For generations, federal policies systematically sought to assimilate and displace Native people and eradicate Native cultures," Biden wrote in the Indigenous Peoples' Day proclamation. "Today, we recognize Indigenous peoples' resilience and strength as well as the immeasurable positive impact that they have made on every aspect of American society." ANALYSIS: Why calls for return of Native land reverberate on Indigenous Peoples Day In a separate proclamation on Columbus Day, Biden praised the role of Italian Americans in U.S. society, but also referenced the violence and harm Columbus and other explorers of the age brought about on the Americas. Landing in what is now the Bahamas on Oct. 12, 1492, Columbus, an Italian, was the first of a wave of European explorers in the Americas pursuing quests for gold and other wealth, including people to enslave. In the course of that quest, Native populations were decimated. "Today, we also acknowledge the painful history of wrongs and atrocities that many European explorers inflicted on Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities," Biden wrote. "It is a measure of our greatness as a Nation that we do not seek to bury these shameful episodes of our past — that we face them honestly, we bring them to the light, and we do all we can to address them." 2a510477f54c.text: By — Emma Burrows, Associated Press Emma Burrows, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nato-commander-says-alliance-does-not-want-war-but-is-ready-to-fight-tonight Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter NATO commander says alliance does not want war but is 'ready to fight tonight' World Oct 12, 2026 1:43 PM EDT WARSAW, Poland (AP) — NATO's top military commander said the alliance is "ready to fight tonight" if it is attacked, as European officials warn Russia could test NATO's defenses with increased covert attacks or a limited military incursion. European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport. If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S. General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw Monday. Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called NATO's "Theory of Victory." The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings." NATO will break the enemy's forces if necessary, Grynkewich says Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack NATO is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces. But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said NATO's combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground. "My theory of victory is simple," he told the Warsaw conference. "We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us." That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said. In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the NATO alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent. Denmark's defense intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the NATO alliance. But, at the same time, President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try lower prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections. WATCH: Poland braces for potential confrontation as Russia tests NATO defenses Earlier this year, the U.S. president said he was pulling American troops from Europe and his war with Iran has led to critical shortages of advanced air defense missiles in Europe. "Ultimately it's a political decision," as to where troops are deployed but "no one should question the U.S. commitment to the alliance," Grynkewich said. It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a "coherent" response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow "where our red lines are." The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine. Some NATO countries still lack readiness to respond to threats While Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning to escalate with drone or rocket strikes on European allies supporting Ukraine, other countries have called for calm. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Agency said there is a "low but growing risk" that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia. NATO does not seek war with anyone but will see a military attack coming and "is unlikely to be caught by surprise," Grynkewich said. Although Grynkewich said NATO would defend against any attack by Russia using a network of sensors and autonomous systems, some NATO nations have previously struggled to perform in exercises simulating drone warfare. They have also faced challenges detecting and responding to incursions of drones which have entered their airspace. Multiple attack drones have crashed in NATO countries bordering Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. And in May, residents in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius were told to seek shelter after a drone strayed into Lithuanian airspace. When asked if NATO could deter Russia in the way Grynkewich described, his spokesperson, Col. Martin O'Donnell said NATO nations are increasingly deploying ground sensors and other technology to detect and counter drones. The network that connects systems to shoot down drones and sensors is in the process of being established, although they have not yet taken down any drones, he said. Western officials blame Moscow for more than 200 incidents since 2022 In September, Germany accused Russia of being behind a plot at Leipzig airport to use a drone laden with explosives to attack a Ukrainian aircraft. British officials also said they thwarted a Russian plot to target a drone facility outside London while Estonian officials said Russia was behind a fire at a defense company. The incidents are among at least 211 blamed on Russia by Western officials since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and tracked by The Associated Press. US actress Selma Blair has been arrested and taken to hospital after authorities say she attacked two flight attendants on a flight.
Airport officials said they responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
The 54-year-old actress, known most famously for her roles in Legally Blonde, Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was taken into custody and transported to hospital. The FBI is investigating.
Blair's publicist told the BBC that she "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".
"Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said.
The incident occurred around 2300 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938.
According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the flight crew allegedly restrained Blair on the flight. Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS includes the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks".
In a statement to the BBC, the FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, confirmed that it is investigating "a potential assault aboard the flight" but would not comment further.
It's unclear whether Blair will face charges relating to the incident. The BBC has contacted New York prosecutors.
A spokesperson for Delta Airlines said that law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident.
"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Airlines said in a statement to the BBC.
Blair largely retreated from film work amid her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis. In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease.
In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board.
She issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret".
"I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time.
US media reported at the time that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and that nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down.
She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital.

But the midterms could decide his future as leader Politics Oct 12, 2026 3:14 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chuck Schumer has won and lost Senate majorities since becoming Democratic leader a decade ago. But this year's midterm elections could be his most important yet, with some in the party having said he needs to step down and make way for a new generation. Schumer, who has directly or indirectly overseen his party's Senate campaign arm in almost every election cycle over the last 20 years, has regained trust within his caucus, for now, as Democrats are hopeful of making gains in the midterm elections despite a difficult map that favors Republicans. Please check your inbox to confirm. Allies of the New York Democrat say it's a significant turnaround from last year, when the party was still reeling from major election losses. A low point came in the spring of 2025, when the party's base erupted at Schumer for voting to keep President Donald Trump's government open. Interviews with more than a dozen Democratic senators in recent weeks indicate that Schumer has recovered his political standing with many in his caucus. If Democrats gain seats in the election, colleagues expect him to easily win enough support in the closed-door leadership election, likely the week after Election Day. Should they win a majority, a feat once seen as improbable, another term as leader would be nearly assured, many said. Both parties pick their Senate leaders by secret ballot, so no senator has to reveal their vote. Still, nothing is guaranteed. While no Democrat has stepped up to challenge Schumer, that could quickly change if his party suffers an unexpected level of losses. And several Democratic candidates around the country have said publicly that they won't vote for Schumer or have remained noncommittal. Interviewed by The Associated Press earlier this month, Schumer stated unequivocally that he's running for another term as leader. He said he believes Democrats have won more favor with voters over the last year and have a shot at winning the majority after fighting Trump's tariffs, forcing more than a dozen votes to end the war in Iran and focusing on affordability, corruption and healthcare. "I think our caucus is strong, it's united," Schumer said. "A year ago, everyone said it was out of reach. Today, we have a broader map, strong candidates, a clear contrast." Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., said that "Senate seats in some ruby red states seem to be in play" because of candidates Schumer recruited. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat who has served with Schumer for almost 30 years, said that "if you had told us in 2025 that we'd be in the home stretch with a really good shot of taking the majority, it would have been like, 'You've got to be kidding me.' You can't argue with results." And if Democrats don't win additional seats? "I'm not thinking about that," Wyden said. Some senators won't commit to supporting Schumer While Schumer appears to be in a good position at the moment, many Democratic senators won't say publicly whether they will support him — particularly those in the most progressive wing of the party. "It's a little bit too early to speculate on that right now," said Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats. Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren said she is focused on November's elections. "We'll know a lot more after the midterms," she said. Freshman Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan has called for a "new generation" of leaders across the party. "It's not a secret that Democrats still haven't totally found their footing after Trump," Slotkin said in a recent interview, adding that "we have to see what the results of the election are." It's unclear if anyone else wants the job Even if there are losses in Senate races, it's unclear if any other Democrat wants the burden of being leader. Many are instead eyeing runs for the White House in 2028. Speculation about a challenge to Schumer has centered on Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Chris Murphy of Connecticut and Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who has already said he's running for the No. 2 leadership spot to replace retiring Illinois Sen. Dick Durbin. Asked about Schumer, Van Hollen said he doesn't want to discuss it yet. "Look, I think everybody wants to get through this election, and then we'll go from there," Van Hollen said in an interview before the Senate left Washington to campaign. Several Senate candidates around the country have either said they won't vote for Schumer if they are elected or remained noncommittal, including Troy Jackson in Maine, Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. At the same time, the Senate Majority PAC, which is closely aligned with Schumer, has put millions of dollars into those campaigns and others. Schumer backed El-Sayed's primary opponent, but the two met in Washington last month. El-Sayed said after the meeting that the party is united and "we're having really productive conversations about what it takes to win." Schumer has kept his caucus close Several of the Democratic senators who insisted on anonymity to share their views agreed that Schumer is likely to win another term as leader. There have been very few discussions about a change, said one, partially because Schumer has stayed close to almost everyone in his caucus, keeping them on speed dial in his famous flip phone. f1ab9c8e2686.text: By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-orders-the-trump-administration-to-cancel-taxpayer-funded-tv-ads Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded TV ads Politics Oct 12, 2026 3:00 PM EDT President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end. U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said. Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as "rather standard" but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow." The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other laws. "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are "available for, among other things, 'commemorating efforts and events related to border security.'" The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration's capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP. "It shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters. The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads. Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent. Associated Press reporters Collin Binkley and Ali Swenson contributed. 079c56a9f9cb.text: By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/high-prices-are-testing-latino-voter-loyalties-in-a-key-battleground-district Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter High prices are testing Latino voter loyalties in a key battleground district Politics Oct 12, 2026 2:41 PM EDT ALLENTOWN, Pa. (AP) — Una sola cosa. Just one thing. That's all Victor Martinez wanted from listeners of his Spanish-language radio station — tell him one positive thing about President Donald Trump. The calls started rolling in. Someone mentioned the $5,000 payout that Trump promised if Republicans keep control of Congress, which Martinez thought was so hilarious that he played a laugh track. Then a trucker shared a silver lining from high diesel prices — he was expecting to take an unplanned vacation because he could no longer afford to fill up his rig. Martinez has been hosting his show for nearly a decade in Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, where Latinos have gone from a fifth to nearly a quarter of the population over the same time period. He added an hour of politics to his morning talk show at the end of Trump's first term, and listeners flooded his phone with their worries about the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, their unhappiness with inflation and their concern over Joe Biden's age. Now, at the halfway mark of Trump's second term, Martinez said people are just as frustrated as they were then. They're angry about higher prices for fuel and groceries, and Republicans could face the consequences in the midterm elections. "It's the economy, stupid. That's what it is. I mean, things have gotten so bad," Martinez said. "People didn't think Biden did a good job. Everything was expensive and now it's worse." Latinos make up a key part of a winning coalition Martinez broadcasts from a fourth floor studio with hardwood floors and a view of an old church in downtown Allentown. He operates the show's control board like an orchestra conductor and sits in front of a poster with campaign signs for Democrats and Republicans. The studio is located in Pennsylvania's 7th Congressional District, where freshman incumbent Ryan Mackenzie faces Democratic challenger Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter and union official, in one of the most closely watched races in the country. WATCH: GOP's big bet on Texas Latino voters could backfire in midterms Latinos are about a quarter of the district's population, and they were a key part of Trump's winning coalition two years ago. Both candidates have organized Latino outreach efforts. Brooks calls himself "Bombero Bob" — Spanish for firefighter — and recently stopped by a Mexican restaurant and a barber shop with a Dominican flag hanging inside. Mackenzie's campaign has promoted support from Latino voters and officials, and the congressman opened a district office in downtown Allentown with Spanish-speaking staff. Martinez is a longtime critic of the president, and this year is backing Brooks. But he said his political roots are in the Republican Party. He supported candidates like Marco Rubio and Jeb Bush, and he opposed Biden's decision to seek reelection because he was too old. Martinez said he uses his show to keep people engaged with politics when some have despaired about the prospect of things getting better. "I got a call yesterday from a guy that said that he was just not going to vote," Martinez said. "I understand that feeling of frustration, but not doing nothing is not the answer." Economic stress looms over the campaign Republicans know Martinez's show is an avenue to reach voters, and they're buying advertising time on it. Jackie Rivera, vice chair of Lehigh County Republicans, said the party wants to hold on to the support from Latino voters that Trump won over two years ago, and that means connecting with them on issues like "faith and family." Although Trump often brags about the economy under his leadership, she said her party wasn't making the same mistake as Democrats did before. "We're not pretending everything is great right now," she said. "You have to be honest with them so that they can believe in you and actually trust in what you're stating to them." Matt Tuerk, Allentown's Democratic mayor, said this year's election has the "same vibes" as two years ago, when Biden was trying to convince people that the economy was strong. "People on the street were like, 'Yeah, but my monthly childcare bill is higher and then my monthly mortgage, the price of groceries is ridiculously high,'" he said. "That's the same story that you hear right now. There's been no improvement." Gas and grocery prices contribute to living 'day by day' Claudia Parrales-DeLeon, a Democratic listener from Allentown, said Martinez's show helps people feel connected as they pay more for gas and groceries and face Trump's immigration crackdown. "I don't know if it makes people less afraid, as much as it makes people more informed," she said. She recalled listening one day when a particular caller's story brought tears to her eyes. "This one gentleman who shared how he just lost his job, he can't find work, doesn't even know where he's going to get his next meal for him and his children," she said. Alberto Pena isn't a regular listener to Martinez, but his concerns are similar. For nearly two decades, Pena and his wife have run a Dominican restaurant in Allentown, where the aroma of crispy pastelillos and savory rice fills the dining room. He voted for Trump hoping he'd turn things around after high inflation under Biden. But they're still "living day by day," and he's leaning toward Brooks this year. "This is not what we expected," he said. "The economy is completely on the ground." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.
So who is saying what?
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.
Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up â if Russia does.
Russia is saying: Very little.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.
"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.
"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."
Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.
It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.
"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.
"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.
"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.
"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.
"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."
In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.
In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.
Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests â as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.
Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel.
Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.
Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.
Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.
It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.
Moscow's reaction?
"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.
"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.
On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.
That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.
It comes as no surprise though.
Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.
Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.
On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.
"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.
The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.
Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

9be41614b6bc.text: By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/authorities-name-the-gunman-and-most-of-the-8-victims-in-last-weeks-erie-mass-shooting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities name the gunman and most of the 8 victims in last week's Erie mass shooting Nation Oct 12, 2026 5:15 PM EDT A coroner on Monday released the names of the gunman and six of the eight people he shot and killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, including seven of his relatives. The shooter in Friday's attack was Matthew Stone Sr., 45, according to Erie County coroner Lyell Cook. Stone took his own life at the home, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said. According to Cook, the adult victims were Michelle Stone, 44; Angelina Stone, 24, who was due to give birth Monday; Jonathan Stone, 19; Matthew Stone, 21, and two women who lived at other addresses: Lora Roberts, 37, and Twila Tanner, 51. He said a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl also died, but that state law prevented him from releasing their names. At a memorial to the victims, Julius Windham said his daughter Amarianna was the toddler who was killed. The girl's mother was Angelina Stone, who was also the mother of the boy who died, he said, noting that attacker was a grandfather and the family patriarch. Family friend Nicole Eller said Roberts frequently went to the house to help during the pregnancy of her niece and neighbor, Angelina Stone. Roberts, identified by friends as a mother of five who was engaged to be married, was a volunteer and former board member for a community group that helped homeless people. She wrote a July 15 Facebook post decrying recent shootings in Erie. "Erie we need to do better!!" she wrote. "Life is precious and its heartbreaking to see so much pain and violence. Check on the people you love, and always choose kindness." Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two "distressed" women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside. Roberts and Tanner, who was the only non-relative, were killed outside the home, Lorah said. The police chief hasn't said what the gunman's possible motives were, but he suggested that his mental health could have been a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh. With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas â and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems.
World affairs seldom provide easy answers, however, and developments elsewhere have threatened to undermine his efforts to bring down fuel prices before they provide any political benefit.
A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months.
High energy prices, particularly for midwestern agricultural states that rely on diesel to power farm machinery and carry their goods to market, have been a growing source of frustration for American voters.
Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously.
Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets.
Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
The truth, however, was more complicated.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of the agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants.
"It's clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelensky noted wryly on Monday. He added: "This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
Trump and Zelensky have had a tumultuous relationship throughout his second term. The American president alternates between blaming Russia and Ukraine for the continuing conflict he previously said would be easy to end once he returned to the White House.
In recent days, Zelensky has been the primary target of Trump's ire, as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have contributed to worldwide energy shortages.
On Saturday, Trump told reporters at the White House that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. And both the Financial Times, external and CNN, external have reported that the US has threatened to cut off arms sales and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Zelensky does not halt attacks on Russian refineries. Zelensky "better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I think that the president has a decade long public record of lashing out of people who aren't doing what he wants, when and how he wants to do it," Terry Haines, founder of independent think-tank Pangaea Policy, told the BBC.
It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements.
Whether it is impatience on the president's part with the slow pace of diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means â and how to react.
Those reactions didn't take long to arrive.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine".
In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course".
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law."
What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon.
Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil.
A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war.
"This is the Houthis sending a message that it's not just military targets, it's not just energy infrastructure, they're going to strike at civilian airports that could kill a lot of people," Michael Ratney, former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told the BBC.
The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in the region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more.
"I do think it gets uglier before it really deescalates," he said.
In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat.

A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.
"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.
Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.
But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.
And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.
