9f9119fc1b2b.text: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting for them to halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. 2880876fc571.text: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.
Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.
Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.
Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.
The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.
Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.
Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.
Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.
It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.
But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.
That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.
Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.
In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.
And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.

5b8b88fec61c.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/kimberly-guilfoyle-trumps-ambassador-to-greece-resigns-after-allegations-of-improper-conduct Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trump's ambassador to Greece, resigns after allegations of improper conduct Politics Oct 13, 2026 12:48 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she'll "vigorously defend" herself. Trump's administration said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. WATCH: Zacharia says White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well." Please check your inbox to confirm. Guilfoyle's departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. "Well, we're looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. "We're not happy." WATCH: 'It was a definite quid pro quo.' GOP donor who accused Guilfoyle of corruption speaks out Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her 'decades of public service' Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in a post on X, saying, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity." "I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations." The allegations began surfacing weeks ago After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied. READ MORE: AP report: Trump, Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports of improper conduct The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation. There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members. Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night," from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie "Barbie." As Trump's family business pulls in record money from new ventures helped by his policies, the survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that when it comes to allegations that Trump is profiting from the presidency, about 6 in 10 U.S. adults believe he is either illegally profiting or doing something unethical but not illegal. Only about 2 in 10 think the Republican president is doing nothing wrong, while a similar share say they don't know enough to say. WATCH: Trump's $2B income in 2025 raises fresh questions about profiting off presidency At the same time, just over half of Americans say Trump has prioritized his personal financial interests "a lot" since returning to the White House, while only about one-quarter say he puts the same emphasis on the country as a whole. "His wealth increases," said 87-year-old retiree Barbara Thaxton, an independent from Summerfield, Florida, "but the people in the country are just barely getting by." Trump derided the issue of conflicts of interest at the start of his second term, telling The New York Times that "I found out that nobody cared." Unlike in his first term, he's lifted a self-imposed ban on his family striking private-sector deals overseas and started several new crypto businesses. WATCH: Trump stock trades fuel accusations of corruption and profiting off presidency The poll results suggest that most U.S. adults think growing his personal fortune has been a focus for Trump in his second term, at least to some extent. Only about one-quarter of U.S. adults say he's prioritizing his personal business interests "only a little" or "not at all," including less than half of Republicans. The White House says Trump is not profiting, but most Americans see red flags The White House has repeatedly dismissed accusations that Trump and his family business are benefiting financially from his office as a fake problem, stating categorically that he has zero conflicts and acts only in the interest of the country. In a required federal disclosure of his financial holdings that Trump filed in June, he reported taking in more than $1 billion from new crypto businesses after he loosened regulation on the industry. WATCH: 'It was a definite quid pro quo.' GOP donor who accused Guilfoyle of corruption speaks out One of his biggest crypto ventures got a half-billion-dollar investment after he was elected from a United Arab Emirates business tied to the royal family. It also got help from a cryptocurrency company founded by a Chinese billionaire in trouble with the law in the U.S. On the real estate side of the business, the Trump Organization has struck eight foreign deals in the first year of his presidency, including many in authoritarian or one-party states with influence over private business and eager to keep Trump happy, U.S. tariffs low or the U.S. military protecting it — or all three. Overall, about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say Trump is doing something illegal, while about 2 in 10 think he's doing something unethical but not illegal. Democrats are especially likely to believe he has broken the law, with about 8 in 10 saying that. Oscar Delgado, a 50-year-old Democrat who voted for Trump in 2024 because he thought he could improve things, now accuses Trump of "turning greedy." "He's not putting the country first," said Delgado, who lives in Lansing, Michigan, and works in a Ford metal stamping factory. "I wanted a change, but I didn't expect this change." Republicans are less convinced Trump is doing something wrong Independents and Republicans are much less convinced than Democrats that Trump is breaking the law. Only about 3 in 10 independents and about 1 in 10 Republicans say he's doing something illegal. About 2 in 10 independents and a similar share of Republicans think his behavior is unethical but not illegal. Most Republicans think he is doing nothing wrong or say they don't know enough to judge. "His family has probably benefited, but I don't think he has," said Republican Audra Pelsue, 52, dismissing Trump critics as too angry to see straight. "It's Trump derangement syndrome." Pelsue, a manager at a laundry machine maker from Syracuse, New York, sees a double standard among Trump critics, pointing to what she says was insufficient outrage over President Joe Biden's son. "Look at Hunter Biden!" she said, referring to his position as director at Ukrainian energy company Burisma when his father, a Democrat, was vice president. "It was OK for Biden kids to benefit, but it's not OK for Trump's?" 66922b338824.text: Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday that she was asked to resign during her first press briefing. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America." Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath. Editor's note: This story has been updated with more information.

Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to Rome's Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove a lump on his lung, detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".
It said the operation would take place on Tuesday afternoon.
The 71-year-old pontiff was met at the hospital by a large crowd, some of whom had been waiting outside for several hours to catch a glimpse of him.
They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, waving and smiling back through the lowered back window of his car.
He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.
It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.
He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The Vatican said the Pope would be operated on by the Gemelli's thoracic surgery team and promised an update on his condition on Tuesday evening.
His schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous. But doctors say when a lump is removed it will usually be tested to check for any sign of the disease.
The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.
He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.
The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.
Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.
"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.
He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.
Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.
Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.
"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."
"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.
"It turns out he's vulnerable too. I really hope it's something superficial, that can be contained, like he told us."

9bcba8da7094.text: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios. Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity. "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says. By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024. New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%. What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom. Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall. "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X . The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.
Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.
The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.
In 1960, researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water. More recently, the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.
Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.
Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.
They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food. They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue. In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.
These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.
The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.
This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.
Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.
Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University. He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.
What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada. “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.
Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.
The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first”  hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”
And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”

cd3f9707a95f.text: By — Mike Stewart, Associated Press Mike Stewart, Associated Press By — Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/police-investigate-mans-fatal-fall-off-six-flags-roller-coaster-in-georgia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man killed on a Six Flags roller coaster was thrown from the ride and hit other patrons, police say Nation Updated on Oct 13, 2026 11:24 AM EDT — Published on Oct 13, 2026 10:49 AM EDT AUSTELL, Ga. (AP) — An Atlanta man killed on a roller coaster at Six Flags over Georgia was thrown from the ride and struck other patrons before landing below, police said Tuesday. The man who died Monday was 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, according to Cobb County police. Visitors at the theme park near Atlanta described watching the man being tossed from the coaster train and falling to his death, causing the theme park operator to temporarily close nine similar roller coasters nationwide. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Several other people were hurt but officials have not released any information about their injuries or conditions. Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the ride associated with the man's death, but local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath roller coaster. The park already was scheduled to be closed Tuesday. One of Goliath's trains remained on its track Tuesday, seemingly where it stopped as it was climbing the ride's first hill. Witnesses describe seeing a man fly out of the roller coaster Logan Conner said he was on Goliath with his fiancée when he saw the man come out of his seat. "The man started levitating in the air sideways," he told NBC. "We made direct eye contact with him." Britny Landry had been on the ride earlier Monday and was waiting in line to go again. "We just look, and I just see somebody fly out," she told KTVU-TV. She said she wasn't sure at first what she saw. "Maybe somebody had a bag or something." Cobb County Police Department detectives are among those investigating. Lisa Cupid, Cobb County Board of Commissioners chairwoman, said the man's next of kin have been notified. "I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Cupid said. "We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories." Six Flags closes roller coasters elsewhere Six Flags Entertainment Corp. temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks "out of an abundance of caution," according to a company spokesperson, who said staff members and local authorities responded immediately and that the park is cooperating with the investigation. "We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said, adding that the company is providing support to guests and staff who were impacted. Police and Six Flags did not immediately respond to messages seeking additional information Tuesday. A message seeking comment also was sent to Georgia's Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees ride inspections. Goliath, which opened in 2006, reaches a top speed of 70 mph (113 kph) with a height of 200 feet (61 meters), according to the park's website. The park in suburban Atlanta opened in 1967. Riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills," during the more than 3-minute ride, the website says. Other recent roller coaster deaths and safety claims The death is at least the seventh at the Georgia park since 1989, including two people who were in restricted areas and struck by roller coasters and two who died in auto accidents, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tallies amusement park accidents and represents victims. In 2006, a man died after likely having a heart attack on the Goliath coaster, the law firm said. The latest death comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California announced the retirement of its X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries. The park settled one wrongful-death lawsuit with the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022. Last year, a 32-year-old man died from blunt impact injuries after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. His death was ruled accidental. "I have cerebral palsy but I've never let it hold me back."
Those are the words of a 22-year-old Breaking Bad star RJ Mitte in an essay for Huffpost, external back in 2014.
Explaining his experiences of learning to stand up to bullies while growing up, he added: "It shouldn't define you. I just happen to have CP."
That was also true of Mitte's character Walter 'Flynn' White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston's character in the drama, which was recently named the best TV show of the 21st Century by the New York Times.
"What I really like is that he was on TV playing a character that had cerebral palsy, but it wasn't about the fact that he had cerebral palsy," says Emma Livingstone, founder and CEO of Up - the Adult Cerebral Palsy Movement.
"When we see RJ Mitte on TV just playing a role, but who also happens to have CP, I think that's really powerful."
Mitte, who died by suicide on Monday at the age of 34, wasn't just an actor - he was also an advocate and supporter, working as an ambassador for charities including United Cerebral Palsy and Can Do Canines, as well as creating The Mitte Foundation, which offered community grants in his home town in Texas.
Susan Sellers, president and CEO of United Cerebral Palsy, says: "His advocacy was rooted in a commitment to ensuring that people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities are seen, heard, and afforded the opportunity to reach their full potential."
Mitte's legacy, particularly for performers with disabilities, is significant.
Ruth Madeley, who stars as disability rights advocate Judy Heumann in new film Being Heumann, tells the BBC: "If you don't see it, you don't think it's possible. When I was younger, acting wasn't even on my radar. I didn't even think it was an option."
The actress, who has spina bifida, adds: "To have people like him [Mitte] on screen for so many young people looking at the arts as an industry that they want to get into... He was just a beautiful example of that.
"But he wasn't just a disabled person breaking down barriers in the industry. He was a phenomenal talent, and I think that's what's going to be missed so much."
Another actor, Keron Day, who appeared in Netflix hit Sex Education, tells the BBC: "My biggest tribute I can pay to RJ and his work is that I am emailing you today from a set of a TV show.
"That is his legacy: disabled people having careers within the creative industries. If I could have half the impact that RJ has had, I would be enormously proud. It's a sad day for both our industry and our community."
Comedian and screenwriter Laurence Clarke concurs. "The more portrayals that we see on TV, that's going to inspire more disabled people to think it's a career for them," he says.
"Things have moved on a long way since Breaking Bad came out in 2008. But there's always further to go."
Speaking of Mitte's role in Breaking Bad, Clarke tells the BBC: "What's beautiful about it is that the disability is visibly there, always."
He also notes the impact on people watching inclusive dramas and shows.
"The more you're exposed to those portrayals, as members of the public, it becomes just part of life, and how you see the world."
Mitte was aged three when he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, which the NHS describes as the name for a group of lifelong conditions that affect movement and co-ordination caused by a problem with the brain that develops around birth.
He was cast in Breaking Bad at 14, and told Channel 4 News in 2016 that the show "pioneered a lot of TV and writers to be more brave".
But he added a note of caution, saying: "We still have a long way to go... it's still a business and we have to do that slowly."
Earlier this month, he hinted that he may be interested in continuing the Breaking Bad story, external, but said any revival would have a lot to live up to.
"I just want to top Breaking Bad, that's the hardest," he said. "I set a bar for myself as a young man that is kinda unattainable. I tell people, 'Look, it's a long way down from the top of the mountain'."
After Breaking Bad, Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.
But his biggest achievement - and his greatest pride - was his philanthropic work.
"Where I felt most top of the world was being able to help others through Breaking Bad, with the work I've done with people with disabilities... trying to remind people they have a voice and [to] lend my voice.
"The greatest thing that Breaking Bad has given me is to be able to lend my voice to causes that make a meaningful impact, that change people's lives."

Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named the leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government.
The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it aimed to coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" in Democratic Republic of Congo and would pursue the goal "by all means, including force".
Its unveiling on Monday is the clearest indication so far of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied having links to the M23 rebel group.
The Congolese government has not commented.
Claude Ibalanky, the coalition's adviser, announced the group's leadership at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which has been under the control of the M23 since last year.
Video released by the group showed Kabila signing documents at the group's declaration along with other leaders.
M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies in the new movement. The other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance which last year seized much of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo.
The announcement of the new group comes days after Kabila delivered an address in which he said he would set out how Congolese people should act to "rescue" their country.
On Friday, Kabila accused President FÃ©lix Tshisekedi's government of disregarding proposals he had put forward last year, including some aimed at ending the conflict in eastern DR Congo.
Kabila also accused the government of undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and failing to improve security. He further alleged arbitrary arrests of political opponents and military officers.
The government has not publicly responded to those claims.
Kabila, 55, ruled DR Congo from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office following a disputed election.
The two were once political allies, forming an informal power-sharing arrangement after the transfer of power. They later fell out and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in 2023 before returning to Goma last year.
The former president had remained largely out of public view for several years but has become increasingly critical of his successor's administration.
The formation of the new coalition comes at an uncertain time in a country that has been wracked by violence for decades.
More than 100 militia groups are active in eastern DR Congo amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
The UN and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing the M23 and controlling the rebels.
Rwanda denies supporting the M23 despite overwhelming evidence, and says its military presence in eastern DR Congo is a defensive measure against threats posed by Congolese armed groups.
Kabila has 'higher profile'
Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028 but in May he said that elections, which are due then, may not be held because of the conflict.
He also hinted that he may seek re-election for a third term "if the people want".
The parliament has since passed a bill that could pave the way for a referendum that could remove the constitution's two-term limit.
Last month, authorities clashed with protesters holding demonstrations in the capital against the proposed changes.
Richard Moncrieff, who monitors Africa's Great Lakes region for the International Crisis Group (ICG) says the new coalition is aimed at trying to enlarge the rebellion.
He argues that through his "higher profile", Kabila hopes to get support from people dissatisfied with Tshisekedi "beyond the very narrow political base that the M23 enjoys".
The analyst says this appears to be Kabila's objective, to draw more senior Congolese army officers to his side and "lessen the reliance of the M23 on its Rwandan backers".
Kabila came to power after the assassination of his father Laurent Kabila, who headed a national rebellion in the 1990s, backed by Rwanda. His forces marched across the country, starting in the east, before taking over in the capital Kinshasa, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) away.
Moncrieff says Kabila is drawing on that past to proclaim the illegitimacy of Tshisekedi's government.
He however says it won't be easy to seize power like his father, partly because the US has imposed sanctions on Kabila, which he says presumes American support for DR Congo's government.
In May the US imposed sweeping sanctions on Kabila, accusing him of backing the M23, providing financial support, encouraging defections from the Congolese army. Kabila said the measures were unjustified and politically motivated.
The US said they were part of a wider effort to support last year's peace deal between DR Congo and Rwanda that it brokered.
The latest events show peace negotiations are "going nowhere and attempting to gain control on the ground is the priority for all parties," the ICG analyst says.

Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.
Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".
Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.
These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.
Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.
The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.
But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.
Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.
While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.
Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information.
The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms".
TomÃ¡Å¡ ZdechovskÃ½, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets."
He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile.
Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform".
They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change".
Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows.
Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.
Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing.
He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded.
Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked.
While there is no evidence to conclude the strikes on Yandex's data centres have had an impact on Russia's influence operations, they have disrupted internet services for many.
Isik Mater, director of research at the internet monitoring group Netblocks, told BBC Verify disruptions related to Ukrainian strikes "affect all users" globally and "websites which rely on Yandex may be partially or entirely unusable".
She said that following Ukraine's attacks there has been a clear impact on the company's cloud services and platforms relying on them, adding that an entire area remaining "out of service indicates a significant infrastructure-level incident rather than a brief service interruption".
Additional reporting by Paul Brown, BBC Verify, and Sergey Goryashko, BBC Russian
Graphics by Tom Shiel

The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other OrbÃ¡n-era laws.
The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism".
Since OrbÃ¡n's April election defeat, the Tisza government of PÃ©ter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy.
Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release â¬4.2bn (Â£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government.
The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds , externaland readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly.
Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that OrbÃ¡n's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation.
"We are very happy that this got adopted," TamÃ¡s Dombos of civil rights group the HÃ¡ttÃ©r Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed."
Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image.
But while Fidesz under Viktor OrbÃ¡n appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality.
In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n to his supporters that he would prevent it happening.
Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions.
The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in OrbÃ¡n's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss.
In his own election campaign, PÃ©ter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters.
"We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side."
This marked a major improvement on the OrbÃ¡n years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents.
"I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities."
Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday.
"There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website.

be2566742294.text:
Timâs view
The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for.
On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv.
The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators, who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference â equal to less than a day of US consumption â and extended a âfinancial lifelineâ to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is âenough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.â
As for the âceasefire,â Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly. A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscowâs behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trumpâs proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries, which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscowâs sights.
Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy canât accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it.
Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Bidenâs decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But itâs counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead.
Notable
- A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of Novemberâs midterms, a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

This week, her creations go on display at Frieze Masters, Frieze Londonâs fair for art made before 2000, where a slot reads as a verdict that the work now belongs to history. Jeddahâs Athr Gallery is debuting with Mosly and a second pioneer of Saudi modernism, Abdulrahman Alsulaiman. Her work hangs in the fairâs Feminist Legacies section.

The News
Inflation tied to the AI boom is âjumping out of its laneâ and starting to push up prices in unrelated corners of the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said.
âPrices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,â he said on Semaforâs Compound Interest. âIâm getting increasingly nervous that thatâs just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.â
Prices for land, electricity, water, construction, and electrical components used in data centers have surged. Those spikes donât appear to have yet hit consumer pain points â for example, the cost of groceries or a haircut â but economists are closely watching how AIâs wealth, from paper millionaires in Silicon Valley to higher-paid construction workers, is being spent.
Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned last month about âsome economy-wide pressure from AI-fueled demandâ but said that so far the boom looks like âa shift in demand toward AI-related sectors rather than an increase in economy-wide demand.â Fighting that kind of sector-specific inflation with rate hikes âcould be a mistake,â she said.
Goolsbee isnât a member of the Fed committee that sets interest rates, but will join it in 2027. He and other economists have been trying to parse how much of todayâs stubborn inflation â 3.4% in August, with Septemberâs numbers due out this week â is from higher oil prices triggered by the war in the Middle East, which the Fed canât do much about, and how much is coming from hotter demand across the economy for goods and services.
âIf inflation remains persistent, then I think itâs clear what the Fed has to do,â he said, when asked whether the central bank should raise interest rates again when it meets later this month.
Lizâs view
The Fedâs problem is that its best tool for fighting inflation doesnât seem to be denting the demand for AI inputs. Hyperscalers arenât slaphappy consumers who might be deterred by higher interest rates. They are locked in a must-win battle and donât seem to mind higher debt costs. Companies like Alphabet and Meta have cash-cow advertising businesses that can support a few extra basis points of interest.
Itâs a broader problem for the Fed: Big parts of the US economy no longer respond to rising interest rates. There may be a pain point for the hyperscalers, but itâs likely to be intolerable for the rest of us.

Iâm engaged in a demystification project about the Federal Reserve. Hereâs what we do. Weâre not the bad guys. Weâre the Guardians of the Galaxy. Iâm going to stay on that for sure.
Liz: Getting to those numbers that you would all like the market to put more stock in and make their own decisions about, even if they were prepared to be weaned off the commentary, does the data that youâre seeing right now lay out a clear picture?
I like how you phrased that. I would say no, not a super clear picture because inflationâs still way too high. I have been worrying publicly about the potential for supply shocks like tariffs, like oil prices to shove us into a stagflationary kind of a trade-off. There is one sense in which it hasnât been ambiguous. It hasnât been stagflationary. The job market still looks very stable to me. Growth has been solid, consumer spending solid. The Houthis firing missiles at Riyadh are not just Iranian proxies â theyâre heirs to a 1,000-year-old Zaydi imamate that ruled northern Yemen on and off until the modern state was established in 1962. Zaydism holds that power belongs to the Prophetâs descendants, not elected officials. In an explainer video, Baraa Shiban, a RUSI fellow who sat on Yemenâs National Dialogue before being exiled for criticizing the groupâs abuses, describes how, after a 1995 trip to Iran, the groupâs founder, Hussein al-Houthi, fused the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam with Tehranâs revolutionary doctrine and built a militia in Hezbollahâs image. The group seized Sanaa in 2014, a decade after its founder was killed.
Rather than replace the state, the Houthis hollowed it out, Shiban said, assigning a âsupervisorâ to sit over every ministry and neighborhood, extorting businesses, indoctrinating the public, and recruiting children as soldiers. They now rule most of Yemenâs population and sit on one of the worldâs busiest shipping lanes.

Both will still do better than Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, whose emir said today that government revenue was down 42% in the first half of the year, because they can pipe crude around the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Fujairah. 524228311da7.text: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The law. A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement , say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws." Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions. Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week. Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country.
A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate.
The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022.
"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement.
The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite".
It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools.
Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country."
The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country.
Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men.
People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers.
The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.

- Published
Barn owl chicks have been ringed in Purbeck for the first time to help track their movements and if the area's conservation-focused farming is working.
The 15 chicks and one adult were ringed at nest sites across three farmland sites in a partnership between Birds of Poole Harbour, Carey Ringing Station and the National Trust.
Mark Singleton, Purbeck's National Trust countryside manager, said: "This is an exciting project and a first for us in Purbeck. Although barn owl numbers have fallen significantly over the past century, there are encouraging signs they may be recovering locally."
Set to run every year, the project hopes to expand with more nest boxes put up next year.
Singleton said National Trust tenant farmers were managing the land to support wildlife with areas of longer grass, maintaining hedgerows and patches of scrub.
He said: "These habitats support the voles and other small mammals that barn owls rely on.
"By monitoring ringed birds over many years, we'll be able to assess how effective these measures are and continually improve what we're doing."
Kate Fox, licenced bird ringer and ornithologist from Carey Ringing Station, said: "Ringing provides invaluable scientific data about these birds, which can't be gained from observations alone.
"Barn owls are striking birds, but it's very difficult to tell individuals apart. If birds move to a different nest box, we won't know whether it's a new pair or birds we've recorded elsewhere unless they have been ringed."
The ringing was carried out under a special licence and follows strict guidance from the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO).
Barn owls are a Schedule 1 breeding species, meaning it is illegal to disturb them during the breeding season without a licence.

- Published
El NiÃ±o has continued to strengthen to what some scientists are calling "unprecedented levels", weeks before its expected peak in December.
Several key measures are now in record territory.
In its latest update, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said average weekly sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached their highest level on record, external.
It comes after scientists declared a new record for daily sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific in September, exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.
Temperatures above 30C have also been recorded for the first time in parts of the tropical Pacific, while record sea-surface temperature anomalies and exceptional subsurface warmth have been observed.
These measurements come from the region of the equatorial Pacific used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
However, the Pacific is also warming due to human-induced climate change and this is starting to mask the strength of the natural warming during El NiÃ±o.
To remove this additional warming signal, Australian and US official forecasters are now using a Relative Ocean El NiÃ±o Index (RONI), to enable better comparison to historical events.
Using that measure, the BOM's average weekly data - while only going back to 2008 - is significant as it now exceeds levels during the record-breaking December of 2015.
"We are currently witnessing an El NiÃ±o event that is unprecedented in the historical record," Dr Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, told the BBC.
Strong El NiÃ±o in a warmer world
The warmth across the Pacific now extends well beyond the tropical region normally used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
Comparisons with previous major events in 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 show much more widespread ocean warmth across the Pacific and into the Gulf of Mexico.
Part of this reflects the long-term warming of the oceans but scientists say it is not the whole story.
"The strength of El NiÃ±o this year is spilling out of the traditional El NiÃ±o region," Dr Hausfather said.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says there is currently no evidence that climate change is making El NiÃ±o events stronger or more frequent, external. However, it remains an active area of scientific research.
What is clearer is that El NiÃ±o releases additional heat from the oceans into the atmosphere.
Historically, global temperatures during El NiÃ±o years are typically higher than during neutral years.
Combined with human-driven climate change, that extra heat is expected to help make 2026 one of the warmest years on record, with unusually high global temperatures likely to continue into 2027.
No two El NiÃ±o events are exactly alike
Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El NiÃ±o's influence is already being felt across parts of the world.
The strength of an El NiÃ±o does not automatically determine the scale of impacts in any one location. Regional effects can vary considerably from one event to another.
However, some common patterns are emerging when compared with previous super El NiÃ±os.
During the 1997-98 event, severe drought across south-east Asia contributed to extensive peat and forest fires, while parts of East Africa experienced devastating floods.
The event also helped make 1998 the warmest year on record at the time.
A similar pattern developed during the 2015-16 El NiÃ±o.
Severe drought and wildfire activity returned to parts of south-east Asia, while southern Africa experienced one of its worst droughts in decades, triggering a major humanitarian crisis.
Another recurring signal is tropical cyclone activity. Strong El NiÃ±o events typically suppress Atlantic hurricanes while boosting activity across parts of the Pacific, a pattern that has also been observed during 2026.
The World Meteorological Organisation says drought and flood-related disruption is already being reported in several regions, with growing concerns over food security in parts of East Africa and the Asia-Pacific.
Forecasts from both the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration indicate El NiÃ±o is likely to peak in December.
Dr Hausfather said the latest projections were "astonishing" and are likely to set new records "by a remarkable amount".

5e3583338dbf.text:
Andyâs view
The Australian sinologist Geremie R. BarmÃ© wrote that âautocrats and patriarchs share a fateful dilemmaâ: Once in power âthe countdown to their demise is on.â
Mao Zedongâs long descent into ill health and madness brought China to the brink of civil war. Deng Xiaoping went out peacefully, though the decade before he died was marked by political upheavals, including the Tiananmen Square protests. Now, the Xi Jinping âdeath watchâ has begun.
Of course, the big difference is that today China is at the center of everything.
As it drags on, the Xi âdeath watchâ will become a global spectacle, moving markets, affecting investment flows, and shaping defense priorities. Chinaâs internal risks are now the worldâs risks.
Xiâs physical condition is one thing. At 73, heâs visibly slowing; he looked fragile descending the stairs of his plane at Air Base Andrews when he arrived for a summit with US President Donald Trump last month, clasping the hand of his wife, Peng Liyuan, for support. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese officials made a highly unusual request for a âhold roomâ for Xi at the White House where he could take breaks between meetings, and his talks with Trump were surprisingly brief.
But the pressures building inside the Chinese system are largely unseen: Leadership politics, including the health of the top man, are as much a black box today as they were in the Deng era. But we can assume that from now on, everything that happens behind the high red walls of the leadership compound in Beijing will be connected, one way or another, to the vexed issue of how a post-Xi China will be governed.
Political transitions are the midnight hour for all autocratic regimes. But Xiâs dilemma is particularly acute: If he names a successor now to carry forward his policies and protect his legacy, he risks triggering a political knife fight years before heâs ready to relinquish power.
Wait too long, though, and he creates a dangerous political vacuum.
Either way, Xi will have to pick a relative unknown â all the current members of the Politburo Standing Committee are too old to step into his shoes â raising a host of troubling questions. Would a designated successor catapulted to the top be strong enough to command the loyalty of the powerful military? Could he hold the Party together?
Or could Xi himself turn on the chosen one? One of Maoâs designated successors, Liu Shaoqi, died of diabetes and pneumonia in solitary confinement, lying in his own filth. Deng cycled through two successors before settling on Jiang Zemin.
Xi has grown paranoid about those around him, his ruthless purges targeting some of his oldest, and most trusted, comrades. That doesnât bode well for any potential second-in-command.
China now faces a period of prolonged political uncertainty.
